docs.text: Status Meaning Accepted when pass On every target of every case of the requirement, the tool reports the rule id on every marked line of every seeded file and nothing on every compliant file, except recorded false positives (listed with the requirement) Always anomaly A recorded false negative of the rule id in any case (or only recorded anomalies), with a log entry and a disposition. The rule id is then partial for the guideline Only for pack and profile queries; the guideline keeps the mitigation the disposition names fail A test does not hold, or did not run on a target Never no test No case for the requirement Never The self-CI fails ( record --check ) when any of these holds: a matrix claim (compiler, clang-tidy) is not pass ; a pack or profile query is fail or no test ; a compliant file draws an unreviewed result; the anomaly log and the cases disagree; the committed record does not match the run.
docs.title: Acceptance criteria

docs.text: Record Where Content Validation record tests/misra-validation/validation-record.json , committed Hashes of the toolchain, suite and matrix; exact tool versions; every requirement with its tests, runs and status Traceability traceability.md , committed Requirement → tests → result; guideline → tools of the matrix, with what is validated Validation report validation-report.md , artifact tool-validation of every self-CI run, attached to each ci-tools release Tool versions and hashes, results by tool, open problems, anomalies with dispositions, limitations, every test result Anomaly log tests/misra-validation/anomalies.yml Every known false negative and false positive, how it was found, its disposition The report is the record an auditor reads. The release attaches the report of the self-CI run that released it.
docs.title: Records

docs.text: A change to any of these changes a validated tool or its configuration: toolchain.json the runner's compiler versions the compile flags a clang-tidy option a case a profile query validate.py the pinned handbook commit (the matrix) Each of these changes the record: its hashes, its versions or its results. The record check then fails the self-CI until the validation has run again and the regenerated record and traceability are committed from that run's tool-validation artifact. A version bump therefore cannot merge without its validation evidence. An update of the runner image that changes a compiler fails the self-CI the same way.
docs.title: Re-validation

docs.text: Validation shows the tools work. Run-time assurance shows they worked on this scan: Canary. A file with known violations ( tools/misra/canary/ru_misra_canary.cpp ) is compiled into every database. If any of its expected query results is missing, the scan fails. Extraction coverage. Every translation unit of compile_commands.json must be in the database. So must every source file under the analysed paths, through some translation unit. An extractor error (severity 4 or 5) fails the scan. Flags. Each translation unit is checked for the org flags. At the safety level, a missing flag fails, because the compiler-decided guidelines would not be enforced. Suppressions. Every marker must cite a record and deviate a finding of that record's guideline.
docs.title: Run-time assurance

docs.text: The review checklist covers what remains: Absence of violations of an undecidable guideline. Passing tests show detection of the seeded forms, not completeness. System-scope guidelines across a whole program, beyond the translation units of the analysed build. Code paths no analysed configuration compiles, today ESP-IDF (Xtensa). The guidelines no tool covers (Dir 0.3.2, and the review-only parts of others).
docs.title: What the tests cannot prove

docs.text: The CodeQL CLI is licensed per user, and only for these purposes: academic research; demonstrating the software; testing OSI-licensed queries; analysis of an Open Source Codebase : a codebase released under an OSI-approved licence; for an Open Source Codebase hosted on GitHub.com, creating databases in automated analysis, CI or CD. The License Restrictions exclude "any codebase that is not an Open Source Codebase". Their own example of such a codebase is a private repository. Those restrictions do not apply under a paid GitHub Advanced Security licence ( terms ). This repository is public and MIT, so the suite runs here and locally. A private driver may not be analysed, in CI or locally, until it is public under its OSI licence, or the organisation buys the licence. ru-misra enforces this before it downloads anything.
